Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette: Thirty years prior, Samir had been twenty-two, laying heavy tar paper on a sprawling industrial warehouse. When the maintenance crew cracked open a neglected ventilation shaft to clear decades of sludge, a thick, sweet-chemical plume rolled over the roof. The wind died. His throat closed. He remembered the stinging in his eyes, the way his boots sank into the hot bitumen as he backed away, lungs burning with a fire that no amount of fresh air could touch. He had stood there until paramedics arrived, coughing into his sleeve, watching the gray cloud linger over the asphalt. The exposure never really left him. Years later, when he was called back to that same site for a roof replacement, he found himself standing at the property line, unable to walk across the gravel. Later, it was the old foreman, a known man who now greeted him at a hardware store, who made Samir step back into the parking lot, suddenly certain that the man's casual conversation carried the ghost of that same air. When the evening news aired a segment about a factory leak in Ohio, Samir found himself muting the television, his pulse jumping to his ears as if the screen itself were exhaling fumes. And then there were the children. His grandson once chased a ball toward a cracked drainage pipe behind their house, and Samir had gripped the porch railing until his knuckles whitened, convinced that the boy's open-mouthed breaths were inhaling something invisible that would make his own lungs seize again. He had never managed to sit down and piece the days together. When he tried to deliberately trace what happened, his mind went flat, like a dry well. Yet when he was washing dishes or staring out the kitchen window, the panic would force its way in without warning. Sometimes it arrived as a physical wave, a crushing terror that filled his chest exactly as it had on that roof, though no picture of the vent or the sky came with it. Other times, it came as a sound or a smell with no source, leaving him pacing the hallway. Even when his wife, Layla, placed a hand on his shoulder to ask about dinner, Samir would flinch so hard his coffee mug rattled against the counter. He was always waiting for the air to turn again. Lying in bed, his shoulders remained drawn up toward his ears. He knew the house was safe, knew the windows were locked, but relaxation felt like a locked door he could not find the key to. He spent hours turning over, counting the minutes between heartbeats, watching the ceiling fan cut through the dark until his eyes burned. Over the years, the habits hardened. He stopped driving past the old industrial district on Route 9. He began taking side streets to avoid the smell of solvents at the home improvement store, eventually asking his daughter to make the purchases for him. At work, he used to walk the ridge lines of commercial buildings without hesitation. Now, when he stood on his own driveway inspecting the flashing around his gutters, he found himself dropping his hands to his sides, suddenly certain that the wind might shift and bring something back. His wife noticed how he no longer laughed during the news, how he slept with the bedroom door cracked open because the dark felt too much like standing on that flat roof with nothing but vapor between him and the sky. At seventy-eight, Samir finally drove to the clinic after a morning when he woke up gasping, his shirt stuck to his chest, convinced the vents downstairs were still pumping. He sat in the waiting room holding a worn folder of old work permits, hoping the doctor might give him a way to quiet the panic, dreading the day it might finally cost him his marriage or his independence.
